title: Investing Foundations
content:
KEY CONCEPTS: Investing is deploying capital today expecting more in the future — distinct from saving (preserving) and speculating (betting on price). Compounding is the core force: returns earning returns, which is why time in the market beats timing the market. The risk-return tradeoff: higher expected returns require accepting higher volatility/uncertainty. Asset classes: stocks (ownership), bonds (lending), real estate, cash, commodities. Inflation is the silent enemy — cash loses ~2-3% purchasing power yearly, so 'safe' cash is a guaranteed slow loss.

WORKED EXAMPLE: $10,000 at 8% for 30 years becomes ~$100,000 — a 10x from compounding, with the last decade adding more than the first two combined. Starting 10 years later (20 years) yields only ~$47,000. The cost of waiting isn't linear; it's the loss of the most powerful final compounding years.

PRACTICE: 1) Calculate what $5,000 grows to at 7% over 25 years. 2) Rank three asset classes by risk. 3) Explain why holding only cash loses money over time.

title: Stocks & Equity Markets
content:
KEY CONCEPTS: A stock is fractional ownership of a business — its long-run value tracks the company's earnings and growth. Price ≠ value: markets swing on emotion short-term, track fundamentals long-term (Graham: 'voting machine short-term, weighing machine long-term'). Key metrics: P/E ratio (price ÷ earnings), dividend yield, market cap, EPS growth. Diversification reduces company-specific risk without reducing expected return — the only 'free lunch' in finance. Index funds capture the market's return at near-zero cost and beat most active managers over time.

WORKED EXAMPLE: An investor picks 'hot' individual stocks and underperforms a simple S&P 500 index fund over a decade — because most stock-pickers, including professionals, fail to beat the index after fees. The boring index quietly won by capturing the whole market's growth at 0.03% cost instead of 1%+ in fees and mistakes.

PRACTICE: 1) Compute a P/E ratio from price and earnings. 2) Explain why diversification is a 'free lunch.' 3) Compare index vs active investing costs over 20 years.

title: Bonds, Fixed Income & Interest Rates
content:
KEY CONCEPTS: A bond is a loan to a government or company that pays interest (coupon) and returns principal at maturity. Bond prices move inversely to interest rates — when rates rise, existing lower-rate bonds fall in value. Yield to maturity (YTM) is the total return if held to maturity. Credit risk (will they repay?) is rated (AAA to junk); higher risk demands higher yield. Duration measures interest-rate sensitivity. Bonds provide income and stability, dampening a portfolio's swings — the ballast to stocks' volatility.

WORKED EXAMPLE: You own a bond paying 3%. Rates rise to 5%. Nobody wants your 3% bond at full price when new ones pay 5%, so its market price drops until its effective yield matches ~5%. This inverse relationship surprises new investors who assume 'safe' bonds can't lose value — they can, when rates rise.

PRACTICE: 1) Explain why bond prices fall when rates rise. 2) Compare a AAA bond vs a junk bond's yield and risk. 3) Describe the role of bonds in a portfolio.

title: Portfolio Construction & Risk
content:
KEY CONCEPTS: Asset allocation (the mix of stocks/bonds/etc.) drives ~90% of portfolio outcomes — far more than individual picks. Modern Portfolio Theory: combining uncorrelated assets reduces risk for a given return (the efficient frontier). Rebalancing (selling winners, buying losers back to target) enforces discipline and 'buy low, sell high.' Risk tolerance depends on time horizon and temperament — young investors can hold more stocks (time to recover); near-retirement needs stability. Dollar-cost averaging (investing fixed amounts regularly) removes timing emotion.

WORKED EXAMPLE: A portfolio is set 70% stocks / 30% bonds. Stocks surge to 80% of the mix. Rebalancing sells the excess stocks (locking gains) and buys bonds — mechanically selling high and buying low, the opposite of what emotion dictates. This discipline, not prediction, drives long-term results.

PRACTICE: 1) Design an allocation for a 25-year-old vs a 60-year-old. 2) Explain how rebalancing enforces buy-low/sell-high. 3) Describe dollar-cost averaging's psychological benefit.

title: Valuation & Analysis
content:
KEY CONCEPTS: Fundamental analysis values a business by its cash flows — Discounted Cash Flow (DCF) sums future cash flows discounted to present value. Relative valuation compares multiples (P/E, EV/EBITDA) to peers. The margin of safety (Graham/Buffett): buy well below estimated intrinsic value to protect against error and bad luck. Moats (durable competitive advantages) justify premium valuations. Technical analysis studies price/volume patterns — useful for timing, weak for long-term value. Beware value traps (cheap for a reason) and story stocks (expensive on hope).

WORKED EXAMPLE: A stock trades at $50; your DCF estimates intrinsic value at $80. The $30 gap is your margin of safety — if you're wrong by 20%, you still don't lose. Buying at intrinsic value ($80) leaves no cushion; buying at $50 means errors and surprises are absorbed. The discipline is buying with a margin, not at fair value.

PRACTICE: 1) Explain the margin of safety concept. 2) Compare two companies using P/E multiples. 3) Identify what makes a business's moat durable.

title: Alternative Investments & Real Estate
content:
KEY CONCEPTS: Beyond stocks/bonds: real estate (rental income + appreciation + leverage + tax benefits), REITs (liquid real estate exposure), private equity, venture capital, commodities, and collectibles. Real estate leverage amplifies both gains and losses — a 20% down payment means a 10% price rise is a 50% return on capital (and a 10% drop is a 50% loss). Illiquidity premium: private assets may pay more for locking up capital. Diversification benefit: alternatives often move differently than public markets. Beware complexity, fees, and illiquidity risks.

WORKED EXAMPLE: You buy a $200,000 property with $40,000 down (20%). It rises 10% to $220,000. Your $20,000 gain on $40,000 invested is a 50% return — leverage multiplied the 10% appreciation fivefold. But if it falls 10%, you lose 50% of your capital. Leverage is a double-edged sword that amplifies the outcome in both directions.

PRACTICE: 1) Calculate the leveraged return on a real estate example. 2) Compare direct property vs a REIT. 3) Explain the illiquidity premium.

title: Grandmaster — Behavioral Finance & Strategy
content:
KEY CONCEPTS: The biggest obstacle to returns is the investor, not the market. Behavioral biases destroy returns: loss aversion (selling winners too early, holding losers), recency bias (chasing recent performance), overconfidence (overtrading), herding (buying tops, selling bottoms), and confirmation bias. The behavior gap: average investors earn far less than the funds they own because they buy high and sell low emotionally. Tax efficiency matters: tax-advantaged accounts, holding periods, and tax-loss harvesting materially boost after-tax returns. A written investment policy statement enforces discipline against emotion.

WORKED EXAMPLE: A fund returns 10% annually over a decade, but its average investor earns 6% — because they poured money in after good years and pulled out after crashes. The 4% 'behavior gap' isn't market risk; it's self-inflicted, caused by buying high and selling low on emotion. Discipline, not intelligence, closes this gap.

PRACTICE: 1) Identify a behavioral bias in your own past decisions. 2) Explain the behavior gap. 3) Write three rules for an investment policy statement.

title: King Level — Wealth Building & Capital Allocation
content:
KEY CONCEPTS: At the highest level, investing becomes lifelong capital allocation — deploying every dollar to its highest risk-adjusted use across a lifetime. Wealth is built by: high savings rate (the biggest lever early), compounding over decades, avoiding catastrophic losses (survival first — you can't compound from zero), and tax/fee minimization. The Kelly criterion guides bet sizing. Sequence-of-returns risk matters near retirement (a crash early in withdrawal is devastating). Estate and generational planning extend compounding beyond one lifetime. The King-level truth: getting rich is about a few good decisions and avoiding ruin, not constant brilliance — protect the downside and let compounding do the work.

WORKED EXAMPLE: Two investors average the same 10% return, but one suffers a single -70% year from over-concentration and never fully recovers (a 70% loss needs a 233% gain to break even). The other never risks ruin, compounds steadily, and ends with far more. Avoiding catastrophic loss matters more than maximizing any single year — survival is the precondition for compounding.

PRACTICE: 1) Explain why avoiding ruin beats maximizing returns. 2) Calculate the gain needed to recover a 50% loss. 3) Identify your single biggest lever (savings rate, fees, or returns) at your life stage.
